title: How Muskrat Ramble grew out of Ory's cornet noodling
summary: Garland says the band added to Ory's cornet figures until it became 'Muscat', retitled Muskrat when recorded; Turetsky compares Ellington's collective composing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Sounded all right. That's how Or got Muskrat Ramble.
How did that start? Orrie wrote Muskrat Ramble, everybody says.
No. I mean, didn't you say that's how Muskrat Ramble started?
Yeah. That's the way Orrie got pretty much 'Muskrat Ramble.'
Because he had a trumpet. It was a -- no, it wasn't a trumpet. It was an old cornet. And he used to be blowing on it. On that thing, you know, trying to play it.
(Imitating sound of cornet.) -- you know? And kept on.
And we all would pitch in and add in to it -- add on to it, you know.
Keep going, adding on to it. That's (Play that again.) how it goes. Every now and then we'd add some more to it, and finally we got to play 'Muskrat Ramble'.
Well, when we got to play it pretty fair, we called it 'Muscat'.
So over at the studios, they corrected that, had that title changed. Instead of Muscat they said Muskrat.
When we went to put it on wax. Called it Muskrat.
Yeah. In fact, that whole way of composing is still alive today. Duke Ellington always did the same thing, you know. Cootie would add something in, or Rex Stewart.
Sure. And I think that's the way to go, working together.
